segments.translation: In the delight of the [joy]{ananda} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} sets out that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as Bhusukupāda setting out 'that same meaning', apparently tying it to what precedes, in the delight of the [joy]{ananda} of [great bliss]{mahasukha} (cp.30.m1).

flags.note: Where Munidatta has tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning' (cp.30.m1), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', as if reading tattvārtham; but de kho na also renders eva, so the Tibetan may be a literal rendering of tam eva. It has rab tu tshim pa, 'thoroughly satisfied', for pramoda, 'delight', and calls the poet 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs, its rendering of Bhusukupāda's name.

segments.translit: karuṇetyādi | karuṇam iti bhāvābhāvaṃ grāhyādivikalpaṃ dalitvā niḥsvabhāvīkṛtya pariśuddhasambhogakāyo yogīndrasya guruprasādaprasphuritaṃ |
segments.translation: '[Compassion]{karuna}' and so on. 'Compassion' means the purified [enjoyment body]{sambhogakaya} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, which, once [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava}, the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of the grasped and the rest, have been split and made [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}, spreads forth by the [guru]{guru}'s [grace]{prasada}.
segments.note: Munidatta glosses 'compassion' as the purified [enjoyment body]{sambhogakaya} of the lord of yogis, spreading forth by the guru's grace once being and nonbeing, which he calls the conceptual thought of the grasped and the rest, have been split and shown to lack intrinsic nature (cp.30.m2). His gloss does not name the cloud.

equations.en: the purified enjoyment body of the lord of yogis, spreading forth by the guru's grace (the gloss stands under karuṇa and does not name the cloud)
the conceptual thought of the grasped and the rest (grāhyādivikalpa), set beside it in apposition

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dngos po dang dngos po med par gzung ba'i rnam par rtog pa, 'the conceptual thought that grasps [things] as things and non-things': it takes being and nonbeing as what is grasped and has no 'and the rest' (ādi). For Munidatta's dalitvā, 'having split' (cp.30.m2), it has sel ba, 'clearing away', as its line 1b has sel for daliyā.

Whose is the enjoyment body? Sanskrit grammar favours taking yogīndrasya with kāyaḥ, 'the enjoyment body of the lord of yogis', since a genitive should not qualify the first member of the compound guruprasādaprasphuritaṃ; I follow that. The Tibetan construes it with the guru: rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug gi bla ma'i drin las 'phro ba, 'spreads forth from the grace of the lord of yogis' guru' (cp.30.m2).

In Munidatta's gloss (cp.30.m2) the neuter prasphuritaṃ does not agree with the masculine pariśuddhasambhogakāyaḥ; I take it as the predicate, 'spreads forth', which the Tibetan 'phro ba'o supports. The absolutive dalitvā (classical dalayitvā) echoes the song's daliyā. grāhyādi, 'the grasped and the rest', presumably means the grasped and the grasper; I have kept it literal.

segments.translit:
ataeva dhruvapadena tasya prabhāvaṃ pratipādayati —
uie ityādi | ataev[ā]gamaḥ
prabhāsva[45ka]re adbhutayuganaddhaphalodayo bhūtaḥ |
tasmāt bho bhusukupāda gurusampradāyāt tṛtīyānande sahajānandasvarūpaṃ paśya jānīhi | svayam eva ātmānaṃ sambodhya vadati |
segments.translation: Therefore with the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he sets out its [power]{prabhava}: 'Has risen' and so on. Hence the understanding: the arising of the [fruit]{phala}, the [wonder]{adbhuta} of [coupled union]{yuganaddha}, has come about in [clear light]{prabhasvara}. Therefore, O [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}, through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, look, in the third [joy]{ananda}, at the [true nature]{svarupa} of [innate joy]{sahajananda}: know it. He speaks addressing himself.
segments.note: Munidatta paraphrases the refrain (cp.30.m3): the fruit, the wonder of coupled union, has arisen in [clear light]{prabhasvara}, where the song has the middle of the sky. He reads 'look' as 'know' and takes the poet to be addressing himself: through the guru's lineage, know the true nature of innate joy in the third joy.

equations.en: know (jānīhi); the Tibetan makes the gloss explicit: ltos shig ni shes par gyis shig

flags.note: Shastri restores ataev[ā]gamaḥ, which gives āgamaḥ, 'scripture'. I read ataevāvagamaḥ, 'hence the understanding', for four reasons: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rtogs pa, 'understanding, realization', the usual equivalent of avagama; Munidatta uses āgama to introduce a quoted verse (tathā cāgamaḥ), and no quotation follows here, only his paraphrase of the refrain; he uses avagamya for understanding a joy in the next comment (cp.30.m5); and the refrain itself asks Bhusuku to look, which he glosses 'know' (cp.30.m3). Caveat: avagamaḥ needs one more letter (va) than Shastri's restoration supplies, so the damaged place would have to hold two signs. Please check the manuscript or a facsimile.
Munidatta cites the refrain as uie (cp.30.m3) where Shastri's song text has uittā; his copy may have read differently, or this is a slip. The Tibetan comment cites it as shar ba, 'risen'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of cp.30.m3: de las de kho na nyid rtogs pa, 'from that, the understanding of reality' (de kho na nyid may render tattva, or eva, as perhaps at cp.30.m1); 'od gsal ya mtshan che ba zung 'jug gi 'bras bu, 'the great wonder, clear light, the fruit of coupled union', with no locative for clear light; bla ma'i drin las, 'by the guru's kindness', for gurusampradāyāt, 'through the guru's lineage'; and it adds rnal 'byor pa, 'yogin', to the vocative.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tasya prabhāvaṃ darśayati —
jāsu ityādi | yasya sahajānandasya pratīkṣaṇe indiālam iti indriyasamūhaṃ truṭyati palāyate |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ |
india jathu vilīa gau ityādi |
nihae iti | nibhṛtena nirvvikalpākāreṇa nijamanaḥ bodhicittaṃ vajraguroḥ prasādāt sahajollāsaṃ dadātīti |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ |
cintācinta parihara ityādi |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he shows its [power]{prabhava}: 'When it is heard' and so on. On beholding that [innate joy]{sahajananda}, 'the [magic show]{indrajala}' (indiāla), meaning the host of the [senses]{indriya}, breaks apart and flees. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'Where the [senses]{indriya} have dissolved and gone…' and so on. 'In stillness' means: quietly, in a form free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}, one's own [mind]{citta}, [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, gives [innate]{sahaja} [delight]{ullasa} by the [grace]{prasada} of the vajra [guru]{guru}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'Give up thought and non-thought…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta takes indiāla, the song's 'magic show', as the host of the senses, which breaks and flees on beholding innate joy, citing Saraha on the senses dissolving (cp.30.m4). One's own mind, [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} (the mind of awakening), in stillness gives innate delight by the vajra guru's grace: a positive where the song line has 'gives no delight'.

equations.en: quietly (nibhṛtena), in a form free of conceptual thought
bodhicitta, set beside it in apposition

citations.work: Saraha, Dohākoṣa (Munidatta names Saraha; the work is my identification)
Saraha, Dohākoṣa (Munidatta names Saraha; the work is my identification)

flags.note: Line 3b reads ṇia mana ṇa de ulāsa, 'one's own mind gives no delight', but Munidatta's sahajollāsaṃ dadāti (cp.30.m4) has the mind give the delight of the innate, with no negative. His wording implies either that his copy of the song lacked ṇa or that he did not take it as a negative. The Tibetan line agrees with him: rang gi yid la dga' ba ster bar byed, 'gives joy to one's own mind', also with no negative, and its comment has lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba ster bar byed, 'gives innate joy'. I have not harmonized: the song draft keeps the negative, and the commentary is translated as it stands.

Munidatta's gloss indiālam iti indriyasamūhaṃ (cp.30.m4) treats indiāla, 'magic show' (indrajāla), as though it came from indriya, 'sense': a reading by sound, backed by Saraha's line on the senses dissolving. The Tibetan comment keeps the image and equates it: mig 'phrul ni dbang po'i tshogs, 'the magic show is the host of the senses'. So the song draft rightly keeps 'magic show' in line 3a, and I keep it in the cited word with indiāla beside it, so the gloss can be followed.

Where the song has sunante, 'on hearing', Munidatta's paraphrase has pratīkṣaṇe, 'on beholding' (cp.30.m4). The Tibetan comment's so sor blta bas, 'by looking at', supports that sense; with a short i, pratikṣaṇe would mean 'at every moment'. The Tibetan line 3a has no hearing at all: gang gi yid la, 'in whose mind'.

Munidatta cites line 3b as nihae (cp.30.m4) where the song has nihure. Where his Sanskrit has nibhṛtena, 'quietly', the Tibetan comment has 'byung bas, 'by arising', perhaps reading a form of bhū, and the Tibetan line has no word for it. In the second Saraha line the Tibetan has sems dang sems med yongs sdud pa, 'mind and no-mind, gathering up wholly', reading citta for cintā and not 'give up'.
In Munidatta's gloss (cp.30.m4) indriyasamūhaṃ, the subject of truṭyati palāyate, has -ṃ where the nominative -ḥ is expected, probably by attraction to the cited indiālam; the sense is unaffected.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena mārgasyānuśaṃsām āha —
viṣayetyādi | yathā candreṇa gaganam udyotitaṃ tathā mayā viṣayāṇāṃ viśuddhyā | ānandeti viramānande paramānandam avagamya tena sahajānandacandreṇa mohāndhakāraṃ nāśitam iti |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}: 'The sense objects' and so on. Just as the [sky]{gagana} is lit up by the [moon]{moon}, so too by me, through the [purity]{visuddhi} of the [sense objects]{visaya}. '[Joy]{ananda}' means: once [supreme joy]{paramananda} has been understood in the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, the [darkness]{andhakara} of [delusion]{moha} has been destroyed by that [moon]{moon} of [innate joy]{sahajananda}.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this verse praise of the path and reads it as a simile: as the moon lights up the sky, so the poet, through the purity of the sense objects (cp.30.m5). 'Joy' is supreme joy understood in the joy of cessation; then the moon of innate joy destroys the darkness of delusion, which this couplet does not name.

equations.en: supreme joy, understood in the joy of cessation

flags.note: For Munidatta's gaganam udyotitaṃ, 'the sky is lit up' (cp.30.m5), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nam mkha' 'od gsal bar byed, 'makes the sky bright, lights up the sky'. Though 'od gsal alone is the Tibetan for clear light (prabhāsvara, as at cp.30.m3), here it is verbal with byed and renders udyotita. It is not evidence that this comment speaks of clear light, and the translation does not mark clear light here.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has khyad par gyi dga' ba dang mchog dga' khong du chud pas, 'by understanding the joy of cessation and supreme joy': two joys joined by 'and', where Munidatta has supreme joy understood in the joy of cessation (cp.30.m5). It also reads mayā as 'my' (bdag gi yul rnams, 'my objects'), like its line 4a (bdag gi dga' ba).

Munidatta's paramānanda (cp.30.m5) may be the technical second of the four joys, or loosely 'the highest joy'; 'understood in the joy of cessation' sits awkwardly with the technical sense. I render 'supreme joy' as the glossary does.

Munidatta's tathā mayā viṣayāṇāṃ viśuddhyā (cp.30.m5) has no verb: the simile supplies 'lit up'; the song's bujhjhia, 'I understood', could supply 'understood' instead. I keep the ellipsis ('so too by me'). His avagamya, 'having understood', in the next sentence picks up bujhjhia.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena[46] phalaprāptitvāt tasya prabhāvam āha —
eteloe ityādi | etasmin trailo(ka)caturthānandavyatirekān nānyopāyo 'sti | yasyodayena siddhācāryyo bhusukupādaḥ | kleśāndhakāraṃ spheṭayati |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
tasmai namo yadudayenetyādi ||30||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada}, since the [fruit]{phala} has been attained, he states its [power]{prabhava}: 'Through these three worlds' and so on. In these [three worlds]{trailokya} there is no other means apart from the fourth [joy]{ananda}, by whose rising the [siddha]{siddha} master [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} dispels the [darkness]{andhakara} of the [afflictions]{klesa}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'Homage to that by whose rising…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the last couplet as stating 'its power' now the fruit is attained: in these three worlds there is no means but the fourth joy, by whose rising the [siddha]{siddha} (accomplished adept) Bhusukupāda dispels the darkness of the afflictions (cp.30.m6). He backs this with a Sanskrit line ascribed to Saraha: 'Homage to that by whose rising…'

citations.work: Saraha (named by Munidatta); a Sanskrit verse, work not identified

flags.note: Where Munidatta has caturthānanda, 'the fourth joy' (cp.30.m6), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dga' ba bzhi dang bral na, 'apart from the four joys': a different reading, or a slip for bzhi pa'i dga' ba. It cites the Saraha line as gang shar de la phyag 'tshal lo, 'homage to that which has arisen'.

In Munidatta's trailo(ka) (cp.30.m6), Shastri's parenthesis supplies ka, but etasmin needs a locative noun; I read etasmin trailoke, 'in these three worlds', as the Tibetan 'jig rten gsum du supports, and take caturthānandavyatirekāt separately.

Munidatta cites line 5a as eteloe (cp.30.m6), running together the song's e tailoe. His paraphrase has nothing for eta biṣārā, 'spreads so far', and his 'no other means' has no word in the line, so it does not settle the sense of 5a. The Tibetan line has rnam par brkyang, 'stretched out'.

questions: cp.30.m3: I read ataevāvagamaḥ, 'hence the understanding', against Shastri's restored ataev[ā]gamaḥ ('scripture'). My grounds: the Tibetan rtogs pa; Munidatta's own avagamya (cp.30.m5); and his use of āgama elsewhere only to introduce a quoted verse, with none following here. The emendation needs one more letter (va) than Shastri's gap-filling. Can the manuscript or a facsimile be checked, and should the edition print the emended text with a note, or Shastri's text?

cp.30.m4 and line 3b: Munidatta's sahajollāsaṃ dadāti (cp.30.m4) and the Tibetan line both have the mind give delight, with no negative. I have left the song draft alone. Should 3b carry a witness flag or note recording that both early witnesses lack the negative?
cp.30.m4 and line 3a: Munidatta paraphrases sunante, 'on hearing', with pratīkṣaṇe, 'on beholding' (cp.30.m4), and the Tibetan line has 'in whose mind' with no hearing. Does 3a need a flag too?
Tibetan de kho na nyid (cp.30.m1, cp.30.m3): should it be treated as 'reality' (tattva, a different reading) or as a literal rendering of eva? My witness flags allow either.

Equations: besides the iti glosses I listed two glosses made by apposition, being and nonbeing as conceptual thought (cp.30.m2) and one's own mind as bodhicitta (cp.30.m4), and Munidatta's 'look', glossed 'know' (cp.30.m3). Keep them, or limit equations to explicit iti glosses?
cp.30.m2: should yogīndrasya go with the enjoyment body, as Sanskrit grammar suggests and I translate, or with the guru, as the Tibetan construes it?
Saraha citations (cp.30.m4, cp.30.m6): I take the two Apabhraṃśa lines to be from his Dohākoṣa (unconfirmed). I could not identify the Sanskrit verse 'tasmai namo yadudayena'.
